system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-02-21 06:28:00 to 2176-02-21 13:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of COPD, chronic alcohol dependence, and tobacco use, was admitted after being found on a park bench with severe shortness of breath and an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. A chest X-ray revealed right middle lobe collapse likely due to mucus plugging, and he was treated for COPD exacerbation with prednisone, azithromycin, and bronchodilators. He was also managed for alcohol withdrawal with diazepam, thiamine, and multivitamins. His right olecranon fracture was noted to have worsened with displacement, and orthopedic follow-up was recommended. Hypertension was controlled with amlodipine. Despite clinical improvement, he left the hospital against medical advice before receiving discharge medications or follow-up instructions.
problems: Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, continuous
Closed fracture of olecranon process of ulna

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. James, I'm Dr. Patel. You're in the hospital again because you came in with shortness of breath and were intoxicated. Do you remember coming to the ER last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was having trouble catching my breath. I think I passed out. I’ve been feeling weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen level was low. We gave you steroids, an antibiotic, and a breathing treatment. Your chest X-ray shows the same right middle lobe collapse we saw before—no change. But there’s no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my lungs are still collapsed? Is that why I can’t breathe well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s part of it. The collapse is likely from mucus blocking the airway. We’re treating you with inhalers and encouraging deep breathing to help open it up. Your breathing has improved since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been smoking much… but I know it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s hard, but quitting would really help your lungs. We’ve given you a prescription for nicotine patches to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also need to talk about your drinking. You were intoxicated when you came in, and your body shows signs of withdrawal. That’s dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… I’ve been trying to cut back. But it’s hard when I’m in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We treated you with diazepam to prevent withdrawal seizures. You’ll need support. We strongly recommend AA meetings. Your sister is listed as your contact—can we involve her?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, she knows… she’s tried to help before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was high this morning, likely from pain and withdrawal. We’ve started you on amlodipine to control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high BP before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, especially with your other conditions. Keeping it under control reduces your risk of heart issues. This pill will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reviewed your right elbow fracture. It’s healing, but you missed your ortho follow-up. They recommend physical therapy and possibly surgery later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot… things get messy when I’m not stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you a 7-day supply of oxycodone for pain until your ortho appointment. After that, you’ll need a primary doctor to manage your pain safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is better now. You’re off oxygen and your lungs are clearer. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel better, but I’m worried about going back out there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But you’re medically stable. You have prescriptions: inhalers, blood pressure meds, nicotine patches, and pain meds for a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should go to AA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and follow up with orthopedics and a primary care doctor. Your sister has your discharge papers. Please reach out to her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We care about your health. Please take the next steps. You can get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check: you’re alert, breathing well, and your vitals are stable. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll call my sister and get to a meeting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’re here if you need us. Take care, James.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try this time.

summary.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of COPD, chronic alcohol dependence, and tobacco use, was readmitted one day after leaving a prior hospitalization against medical advice. He presented with shortness of breath and acute intoxication. He was treated for COPD exacerbation with prednisone, azithromycin, and bronchodilators, and his oxygen levels improved to the mid-90s on room air. His right middle lobe collapse remained unchanged on chest X-ray. He received diazepam for alcohol withdrawal and was encouraged to attend AA. Hypertension was managed with amlodipine. He was discharged home with a short-term oxycodone prescription for his right olecranon fracture pain, instructions to follow up with orthopedics and physical therapy, and a nicotine patch prescription to aid smoking cessation. He left with improved respiratory status and a plan for outpatient care.
